Part 1 defined vectors on a manifold as directional derivatives. Physics needs more than vectors. The electromagnetic
field, the stress inside a material, and the curvature of spacetime are all quantities that take several directions
and return a number. Tensors are the general framework for such quantities, and the only one in which laws can be
written without reference to a choice of coordinates.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Background: metrics

[Metrics: From Distance to the Metric Tensor](/explainers/metrics/) explains the two meanings of "metric", how an inner
product becomes a matrix of components, and how the same space looks in different charts, with an interactive explorer.
:::

## Covectors

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Definition

The **cotangent space** $T^*_pM$ is the dual of $T_pM$: the vector space of linear maps $\omega: T_pM \to \mathbb{R}$.
Its elements are **covectors** (also called one-forms or dual vectors).
:::

The basic example is the **differential** of a function. For $f \in C^\infty(M)$, define

$$
df_p(V) = V(f).
$$

It eats a direction and returns the rate of change of $f$ in that direction: it is the gradient, made coordinate-free.

The differentials of the coordinate functions are a basis of $T^*_pM$, dual to the basis $\partial_\mu$:

$$
dx^\mu(\partial_\nu) = \partial_\nu x^\mu = \delta^\mu_{\ \nu},
$$

where $\delta^\mu_{\ \nu}$ is 1 when $\mu = \nu$ and 0 otherwise. Any covector can be written $\omega = \omega_\mu dx^\mu$,
with components $\omega_\mu = \omega(\partial_\mu)$, and then $df = \partial_\mu f\,dx^\mu$: the components of $df$ are the
partial derivatives of $f$.

A covector applied to a vector gives $\omega(V) = \omega_\mu V^\mu$. Applying a covector to a vector, or a vector to a
covector, are the same pairing, and needs no metric.

**Transformation law.** Since $dx^\nu = \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'^\mu} dx'^\mu$,

$$
\boxed{\omega'_\mu = \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'^\mu}\,\omega_\nu .}
$$

This is the inverse of the vector law. Vector components transform with the matrix $\partial x'/\partial x$, covector
components with $\partial x/\partial x'$, so that the number $\omega_\mu V^\mu$ is the same in every chart. That is why
vector components carry their index up and covector components down: a summed pair of indices, one up and one down,
always makes something independent of coordinates.

![Left: the polar coordinate basis vectors on the plane. ∂r has unit length everywhere; ∂φ points round the circles and has length r. Right: a covector can be drawn as a family of level sets. Here dφ has level sets on the rays φ = constant, and its value on a vector V counts how many of them V crosses. Near the origin the rays are close together, so dφ is large: its length is 1/r.](fig_polar_basis.png)

## Tensors

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Definition

A **tensor of type $(k, l)$** at $p$ is a multilinear map
$$
T: \underbrace{T^*_pM \times \dots \times T^*_pM}_{k} \times \underbrace{T_pM \times \dots \times T_pM}_{l} \to \mathbb{R}.
$$
It takes $k$ covectors and $l$ vectors, and is linear in each argument separately. A **tensor field** assigns one to
each point, smoothly.
:::

Some familiar cases:

| Type | Object | Example in general relativity |
|:--|:--|:--|
| (0, 0) | scalar | temperature, proper time along a curve |
| (1, 0) | vector | four-velocity |
| (0, 1) | covector | gradient of a scalar field |
| (0, 2) | bilinear form | the metric $g$ (Part 3) |
| (1, 1) | linear map $T_pM \to T_pM$ | the identity $\delta^\mu_{\ \nu}$ |
| (2, 0) | | the inverse metric $g^{\mu\nu}$ |
| (1, 3) | | the Riemann curvature tensor (Part 5) |

**Tensor product.** If $S$ is of type $(k, l)$ and $T$ of type $(m, n)$, then $S \otimes T$ is the $(k + m, l + n)$
tensor that feeds the first arguments to $S$, the rest to $T$, and multiplies the results. Products of basis elements
give a basis:

$$
T = T^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_k}{}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_l}\;
\partial_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \partial_{\mu_k} \otimes dx^{\nu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{\nu_l},
$$

with components $T^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_k}{}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_l} = T(dx^{\mu_1}, \dots, dx^{\mu_k}, \partial_{\nu_1}, \dots, \partial_{\nu_l})$.
In $n$ dimensions, a type $(k, l)$ tensor has $n^{k+l}$ components. The Riemann tensor in four dimensions has 256,
though its symmetries cut the independent ones to 20 (Part 5).

**Transformation law.** Each index transforms as its type requires, independently:

$$
T'^{\mu}{}_{\nu} = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\alpha}\frac{\partial x^\beta}{\partial x'^\nu}\,T^{\alpha}{}_{\beta},
$$

and similarly for any number of indices. This follows directly from the multilinear definition, by expanding each basis
element in the new basis.

## Why physics is written in tensors

Suppose a law takes the form $T^{\mu}{}_{\nu} = 0$ in some chart. In any other chart, the transformation law gives
$T'^{\mu}{}_{\nu}$ as a linear combination of the components $T^{\alpha}{}_{\beta}$, all of which vanish. So
$T'^{\mu}{}_{\nu} = 0$ too.

More generally, if two tensors are equal in one chart, they are equal in all. A law of physics written as an equation
between tensors is automatically independent of the coordinates used to describe it. This is the precise content of
**general covariance**, and the reason Einstein spent years learning tensor calculus from his friend Marcel Grossmann.

## Operations on tensors

**Contraction.** Summing an upper index against a lower one reduces type $(k, l)$ to $(k - 1, l - 1)$:

$$
S^{\mu}{}_{\nu\rho} \;\longmapsto\; S^{\mu}{}_{\mu\rho}.
$$

The result is a tensor: the transformation matrices of the two contracted indices are inverse to each other and cancel.
The trace of a matrix is the simplest contraction. Contracting two indices of the same kind, both up or both down, is
not allowed without a metric, and does not give a tensor.

**Symmetry.** A $(0, 2)$ tensor splits into symmetric and antisymmetric parts:

$$
T_{\mu\nu} = T_{(\mu\nu)} + T_{[\mu\nu]}, \qquad
T_{(\mu\nu)} = \tfrac12(T_{\mu\nu} + T_{\nu\mu}), \qquad
T_{[\mu\nu]} = \tfrac12(T_{\mu\nu} - T_{\nu\mu}).
$$

Symmetry is preserved by change of coordinates. The metric is symmetric. The electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu\nu}$
is antisymmetric. Totally antisymmetric $(0, p)$ tensors, the **differential forms**, have their own calculus, with the
exterior derivative $d$ generalising grad, curl and div.

**Index rules.** Every valid tensor equation obeys three rules, which make errors easy to spot:

1. each free (unsummed) index appears exactly once in every term, at the same height;
2. each summed (dummy) index appears exactly twice in a term, once up and once down;
3. dummy indices can be renamed freely: $V^\mu\omega_\mu = V^\nu\omega_\nu$.

## Not everything with indices is a tensor

**Tensor densities.** The Levi-Civita symbol $\tilde\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$, equal to $\pm 1$ or $0$ according to
the permutation of its indices, has the same components in every chart, so it does not transform as a tensor. Under a
change of coordinates it picks up a factor of the Jacobian determinant. Such objects are **tensor densities**. With a
metric, they can be converted into true tensors, and $\sqrt{|\det g|}\, d^4x$ becomes the invariant volume element used
to write the action of general relativity.

**The partial derivative of a vector.** This is the important failure. Take the components $\partial_\mu V^\nu$ and
change coordinates:

$$
\partial'_\mu V'^\nu
= \frac{\partial x^\alpha}{\partial x'^\mu}\partial_\alpha\!\left(\frac{\partial x'^\nu}{\partial x^\beta} V^\beta\right)
= \frac{\partial x^\alpha}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial x'^\nu}{\partial x^\beta}\,\partial_\alpha V^\beta
\;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial x^\alpha}{\partial x'^\mu}\frac{\partial^2 x'^\nu}{\partial x^\alpha\,\partial x^\beta}\,V^\beta}_{\text{not tensorial}} .
$$

The first term is the tensor law. The second appears whenever the transformation is not linear, which on a curved
manifold is always. The reason is geometric: $\partial_\mu V^\nu$ compares the vector at two neighbouring points, but
those vectors live in different tangent spaces, and the manifold provides no way to compare them.

The polar plane shows it plainly. The constant vector field $\partial_x$ has polar components
$(\cos\phi, -\sin\phi/r)$, which vary from point to point, so their partial derivatives are not zero, although the field
does not change at all. Fixing this needs an extra structure, a **connection**, which says how to carry a vector from
one tangent space to the next. That is Part 4. First, Part 3 adds the metric, which, among other things, picks out a
natural connection.

## Summary

- Covectors are linear maps on vectors. The differentials $dx^\mu$ form the basis dual to $\partial_\mu$.
- A type $(k, l)$ tensor is a multilinear map of $k$ covectors and $l$ vectors. Its components transform with one
  factor of $\partial x'/\partial x$ per upper index and one of $\partial x/\partial x'$ per lower index.
- An equation between tensors holds in every chart if it holds in one: general covariance.
- Contraction and symmetrisation give new tensors. The Levi-Civita symbol is a density, not a tensor.
- The partial derivative of a vector field is not a tensor, because it compares vectors in different tangent spaces.
